title: Counts, Person-Time, Rate, and the Offset

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Recall §1.5 and §7.4.1: a rate divides a count of events by person-time at risk, while an incidence proportion (risk) divides by the number of people at risk over a fixed period. An offset is a term, log(person-time) or log(population), entered into a Poisson model with its coefficient fixed at 1. It makes the model describe rates instead of raw counts.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Two villages report malaria cases this year: Village A had 40 cases among 4,000 people, Village B had 20 among 500. Village B’s incidence proportion (20/500 = 4%) is four times Village A’s (40/4,000 = 1%), despite half the count. A count is comparable across nothing until its denominator is known.

A Poisson model (§13.5) models the log of an expected count. Without an offset it compares raw counts, as if every village had the same population and follow-up. The offset tells the model how much opportunity each unit had.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
For unit i with person-time Tᵢ and rate λᵢ, the expected count is μᵢ = λᵢTᵢ. Model the log rate linearly: log λᵢ = b₀ + b₁xᵢ. Then

log μᵢ = log Tᵢ + b₀ + b₁xᵢ.

The term log Tᵢ has no coefficient to estimate (it is fixed at 1). That is the offset. Subtracting it gives log(μᵢ/Tᵢ) = b₀ + b₁xᵢ: the model is for the log rate, although the outcome fed to the software is the raw count. For a binary x, e^(b₁) = λ(x = 1)/λ(x = 0), the incidence rate ratio (IRR).

Without the offset, e^(b₁) is the ratio of expected counts. It equals the rate ratio only if every unit had the same Tᵢ.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Ten villages report malaria cases for one year (data/malaria_villages.csv). Five lie near standing water (191 cases among 9,500 people) and five do not (118 cases among 13,500 people). The villages near water are also smaller on average.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Rate near water = 191/9,500 = 20.1 per 1,000 per year. Rate elsewhere = 118/13,500 = 8.74 per 1,000.
  2. IRR = 20.1 ÷ 8.74 = 2.30. SE(ln IRR) = √(1/191 + 1/118) = 0.117 (recall §7.4.4), so 95% CI = 1.83 to 2.89.
  3. Without the population offset, the model compares mean cases per village: 191/5 = 38.2 against 118/5 = 23.6, a count ratio of 1.62. Ignoring the populations understates the difference in rates, because the villages near water have fewer people.

points.html: The offset is log(person-time) or log(population), with its coefficient fixed at 1. With it, exp(b) is a rate ratio; without it, a count ratio. Check which before you read a Poisson coefficient. (§13.5 and §13.6 rely on this and do not repeat it.)
The unit of person-time sets the unit of the rate, not the rate ratio.
